Living Well / Practical guide

Preserve a family story without losing the person's voice

Practical guide · 5 min read · Published October 8, 2026

Revision, 2026-10-09: Added a small hypothetical first project and linked free conversation and preservation resources.

On this page
  1. Start with the story they want to tell
  2. Agree on the boundaries before recording
  3. Make the technology quiet enough to listen
  4. Keep an original and make edits traceable
  5. Let the person review the version that will be shared
  6. Preservation is more than storage
  7. Start with one story, not an entire archive
  8. One question to take with you

The goal is not merely to produce a polished file. It is to listen carefully and preserve a story in a form the person recognizes as their own.

Start with the story they want to tell

Invite a person to talk about something they would like remembered. A familiar object, an ordinary job, a family meal, or a place they once knew may be a better opening than a demand to summarize their entire life. They can decline, change the subject, or prefer an unrecorded conversation.

Ask who the story is for. A private keepsake, a family gathering, and a public website are different projects. The Oral History Association's ethics guidance emphasizes informed participation, clarity about intended use, and an opportunity for narrator review. The practical sequence here is an editorial adaptation for a small family project, not a legal consent form.

Agree on the boundaries before recording

Discuss whether to record or take notes, what subjects to avoid, who may access the material, where copies will be stored, and what the speaker will review. Ask separately about third-party transcription or AI assistance. Permission to speak into your recorder is not automatically permission to upload the recording elsewhere.

Be honest about what you can control. Do not promise that a publicly shared file can always be fully recalled. A private conversation may be the right choice, particularly when other people's sensitive experiences are involved. The family-story worksheet helps organize this discussion without claiming to settle legal rights.

Make the technology quiet enough to listen

Use a setup you understand. Make a short test recording with permission and play it back. Check that the speaker can be heard, that the device has room and power, and that the surroundings suit the conversation. The simplest reliable setup is preferable to an elaborate one that occupies your attention.

Prepare a few open questions rather than a rigid script. What was an ordinary day like? What did you misunderstand at the time? What detail do you wish people remembered? Follow the answer that interests the speaker. Do not steer every memory toward a lesson or a dramatic emotional reveal.

Keep an original and make edits traceable

Preserve the original recording separately from working copies. If you create a transcript, treat it as something to check against the recording. Mark uncertain passages instead of guessing. Keep names, dates, and factual questions visible for review.

When using an agreed transcription service, inspect its current privacy and retention arrangements first. Ask a tool to mark uncertainty, not invent missing words. Do not automatically smooth away expressions that matter to the speaker. A clearer paragraph is not necessarily a more faithful account.

An optional, limited request is: Using only this approved excerpt, identify unclear words and suggest a readable layout. Do not add facts, imitate missing speech, or change the speaker's meaning. Separate every proposed correction from the original. Review the result yourself and with the speaker.

Let the person review the version that will be shared

Show the actual transcript, edited audio, or selected excerpt, not merely a description of the project. Ask whether the wording feels accurate, what context is missing, and which parts should stay private. Keep their preferences about attribution and audience with the project files.

A family disagreement about an event does not require silently rewriting the speaker's memory into someone else's version. Distinguish the recollection from independently checked facts. You can preserve an account while noting uncertainty, rather than claiming to have created a complete historical record.

Preservation is more than storage

Use understandable file names and keep a short note explaining who is speaking, when the conversation took place, and what permissions apply. Keep a backup in an agreed location and check that the files open. The Oral History Association's best practices discuss preparation, preservation, and access as connected responsibilities.

Then consider how the story will actually be encountered. A short excerpt shared with permission at a gathering, a simple printed page, or a recording someone knows how to find may be more useful than an elaborate archive nobody can navigate. Remembering a person also involves listening, retelling responsibly, and making room for what they cared about.

Do not clone the person's voice or create new speech in their name as part of this process. Preserving a story is different from generating things the person never said. The Library of Congress introduction to preserving family stories offers further prompts and examples of oral-history work.

Start with one story, not an entire archive

Hypothetical example: Someone in a family would like to tell the story of an object they have kept for years. The object and speaker are invented for this example. You ask whether they would enjoy a short conversation and whether they prefer notes, audio, or simply talking.

Agree on one audience, such as the people already in the conversation. Ask what they would like remembered about the object and follow the detail they choose. If they do not want a record, the conversation itself is enough. The public StoryCorps question bank offers other openings, but there is no requirement to ask anything intrusive.

With their agreement, make one simple record and let them check it. Name the file so a person can understand it later, keep the original separate from an edited copy, and save an agreed backup. The Library of Congress preservation guidance provides a starting point; older software examples need checking against current instructions.

The first project can end with a single reviewed page or short recording. Permission to share it with one relative does not become permission to publish it on a website or upload it to an AI service. A story does not need a public audience to be worth preserving.

One optional practice

Invite someone to discuss one story they would like preserved. Start with permission and their preferred audience. A useful first outcome is agreement about the project, even if no recording is made that day.

Keep any notes privately. Skip or adapt this exercise if it does not fit your circumstances.

One question to take with you

Will the person whose story this is recognize both their voice and their choices in the result?
